<reason>B more convincingly separated pricing’s incremental benefits from those of ordinary curb management. A established a plausible incentive for flexible trips to reschedule, but B’s reservation alternative weakened the circling comparison, and B directly rebutted claims that only prices reveal shortages or permit adjustment. A’s answer to the cap-versus-inelastic-demand question remained unresolved. The permissive “allow” framing helped A, but did not establish that variable charges improve the managed alternative enough to outweigh the access burdens.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B decisively challenged A’s closing claim of “a tie in the worst case and a win everywhere else”: inflexible trips face unchanged scarcity plus a charge, while profitable discretionary stops may absorb fees that exclude necessary low-margin deliveries. This exposed A’s unsupported equation of price responsiveness with priority of access.</best_rebuttal>
